source_text: Audio poetas quoque « unum patrem divum atque hominum » praedicantes, et « talem esse mortalium mentem qualem parens omnium diem duxerit. » Quid Mantuanus Maro? nonne apertius, proximius, verius? « Principio, ait, coelum et terras, » et caetera mundi membra « spiritus intus alit, et infusa mens agitat. Inde hominum pecudumque genus » et quidquid aliud animalium. Idem alio loco, mentem istam et spiritum, Deum nominat; haec enim vera sunt: Deum namque ire per omnes Terrasque tractusque maris coelumque profundum. Unde homines, et pecudes, unde imber et ignis. Quid aliud et a nobis Deus, quam mens et ratio et spiritus praedicatur? Recenseamus, si placet, disciplinas philosophorum, deprehendes eos, etsi sermonibus variis, ipsis tamen rebus in hanc unam coire et conspirare sententiam. (XII) Omitto illos rudes et veteres qui de suis dictis sapientes esse meruerunt. Sit Thales Milesius omnium primus, qui primus omnium de coelestibus disputavit. Is Milesius Thales rerum initium aquam dixit; Deum autem eam mentem quae ex aqua cuncta formaverit. Eho! altior et sublimior aquae et spiritus ratio, quam ab homine potuerit inveniri; a Deo traditum. Vides Philosophi principalis nobiscum penitus opinionem consonare. Anaximenes deinceps, et post Apolloniates Diogenes, aera Deum statuunt, infinitum et immensum. Horum quoque similis de divinitate consensio est. Anaxagorae vero descriptio et motus infinitae mentis Deus dicitur. Et Pythagorae Deus est animus, per universam rerum naturam commeans et intentus: ex quo etiam animalium omnium vita capiatur. Xenophanem notum est omne infinitum cum mente Deum tradere; et Antisthenem, populares deos multos, sed naturalem unum praecipuum; Zeuxippum [ imp. Spensippum], vim naturalem, animalem, qua omnia regantur, Deum nosse. Quid Democritus? quamvis atomorum primus inventor,26 nonne plerumque naturam, quae imagines fundat, et intelligentiam, Deum loquitur? Straton quoque et ipse naturam: etiam Epicurus ille qui deos aut otiosos fingit aut nullos, naturam tamen superponit. Aristoteles variat, et adsignat tamen unam potestatem. Nam interim mentem, mundum interim Deum dicit, interim mundo Deum praeficit. Aristoteles Ponticus variat, alias mundo, alias menti divinae tribuens principatum. Heraclides Ponticus quoque Deo divinam mentem, quamvis varie, adscribit. Theophrastus, et Zenon, et Chrysippus, et Cleanthes, sunt et ipsi multiformes; sed ad unitatem providentiae omnes revolvuntur. Cleanthes enim mentem, modo animum, modo aethera, plerumque rationem Deum disseruit. Zenon, ejusdem magister, naturalem legem atque divinam, et aethera interim, interdumque rationem, vult omnium esse principium. Item interpretando Junonem aera, Jovem coelum, Neptunum mare, ignem esse Vulcanum, et caeteros similiter vulgi deos elementa esse monstrando, publicum arguit graviter et revincit errorem. Eadem fere Chrysippus, vim divinam, rationalem naturam, et mundum interim, et fatalem necessitatem Deum credit, Zenonemque interpretatione physiologiae in Hesiodi, Homeri Orpheique carminibus imitatur. (XIII) Babylonio etiam Diogeni disciplina est exponendi et disserendi Jovis partum et ortum Minervae, et hoc genus caeterarum rerum vocabula esse, non deorum. (XIV) Nam Socraticus Xenophon formam Dei veri negat videri posse, et ideo quaeri non oportere. Aristo Stoicus , comprehendi omnino non posse. Uterque majestatem Dei, intelligendi desperatione; senserunt. Platoni apertior de Deo et rebus ipsis et nominibus oratio est; et quae tota esset coelestis, nisi persuasionis civilis nonnumquam admixtione sordesceret. Platoni itaque in Timaeo Deus est ipso suo nomine mundi parens, artifex animae, coelestium terrenorumque fabricator; quem et invenire difficile, prae nimia et incredibili potestate; et, cum inveneris, in publicum dicere impossibile praefatur. (XV) Eadem fere et ista quae nostra sunt nam et Deum novimus et parentem omnium dicimus, et numquam publice, nisi interrogati, praedicamus.
thought_title: Poets and Philosophers on God's Unity
pass_a_gloss: I hear that the poets also preach that there is one father of gods and men, and that the mind of mortals is such as the parent of all things has deemed it to be. What about the Mantuan Maro? Does he not say more openly, more closely, and more truly? In the beginning, he says, heaven and earth and the other parts of the world are nourished by a spirit within and a mind that has been infused, and from this comes the race of men and beasts and whatever other animals. In another place, he calls this mind and spirit God; for it is true that God goes through all lands and tracts of sea and deep heaven. From him come men and beasts, from him come rain and fire. What else do we preach about God, except that he is mind and reason and spirit? Let us review, if you please, the teachings of the philosophers, and you will find that they, although they use different words, nevertheless come to the same conclusion and agree on this one opinion. I pass over those rude and ancient ones who have been considered wise because of their sayings. Let Thales of Miletus be the first of all, who first of all discussed heavenly things. This Thales of Miletus said that the beginning of things is water, but that God is the mind that has formed all things from water. Behold, a higher and more sublime reason of water and spirit than could have been discovered by man; it was handed down by God. You see that the principal opinion of the philosopher is in complete agreement with ours. Anaximenes, and after him Diogenes of Apollonia, establish air as God, infinite and immense. The consensus of these men about divinity is also similar. Anaxagoras indeed calls the description and motion of the infinite mind God. And Pythagoras says that God is the soul that goes through the whole nature of things and is intent on it; from which also the life of all animals is derived. It is well known that Xenophanes hands down that all infinite things are God with mind; and Antisthenes, that there are many popular gods, but one natural and principal god; and Zeuxippus, that the natural, animal power by which all things are ruled is known as God. What about Democritus? Although he was the first inventor of atoms, does he not often speak of nature, which founds images, and intelligence, as God? Strato also, and even Epicurus, who either imagines gods as idle or as non-existent, nevertheless places nature above them. Aristotle varies, but nevertheless assigns one power; for he sometimes calls the mind God, sometimes the world, and sometimes places God over the world. Aristotle of Pontus also varies, sometimes attributing the principle to the world, sometimes to the divine mind. Heraclides of Pontus also ascribes the divine mind to God, although in various ways. Theophrastus, and Zeno, and Chrysippus, and Cleanthes, are also multiform; but they all return to the unity of providence. For Cleanthes discusses God as mind, sometimes as soul, sometimes as ether, and often as reason. Zeno, his master, wants the natural law and the divine law, and sometimes ether, and sometimes reason, to be the principle of all things. Similarly, by interpreting Juno as air, Jupiter as heaven, Neptune as sea, and fire as Vulcan, and showing that the other popular gods are elements, he seriously accuses and overcomes the error. Chrysippus also believes that the divine power, the rational nature, and the world, and the fatal necessity, are God, and imitates Zeno in the physiological interpretation of the songs of Hesiod, Homer, and Orpheus. The Babylonian Diogenes also has the discipline of explaining and discussing the birth and origin of Jupiter and Minerva, and that these and other such words are not about gods. For the Socratic Xenophon denies that the form of the true God can be seen, and therefore should not be sought. The Stoic Aristo says that it cannot be comprehended at all. Both of them, in their desperation to understand, have sensed the majesty of God. Plato's speech about God and things themselves and their names is more open; and it would be entirely heavenly, if it were not sometimes sullied by the admixture of civil persuasion. Therefore, in the Timaeus, God is the parent of the world, the artisan of the soul, the fabricator of heavenly and earthly things; whom it is difficult to find, because of his too great and incredible power; and when you have found him, it is impossible to speak of him publicly, he says. We also have similar things, for we know God and call him the parent of all, and we never preach publicly, unless we are asked.

pass_b_english: I hear the poets also proclaim one Father of gods and men, and that the mind of mortals takes its character from whatever day the Parent of all has ordained (Virgil, Aeneid 6.724–725). What of the Mantuan Maro? Does he not speak more openly, more directly, more truly? "In the beginning," he says, "heaven and earth" and the rest of the world's members "are nourished by a spirit within, and an infused mind stirs them. From this comes the race of men and beasts, and every other kind of animal" (Aeneid 6.724–727). Elsewhere he names that mind and spirit God; for it is true: "God goes through all lands and tracts of sea and deep heaven. From him come men and beasts, from him come rain and fire" (Aeneid 6.727–729). What else do we proclaim about God but that he is mind, reason, and spirit? Let us review, if you please, the teachings of the philosophers, and you will find that, for all their different vocabularies, they converge on this single conclusion. I pass over those crude ancients who earned a reputation for wisdom merely through their sayings. Take Thales of Miletus as the first, the first to debate heavenly matters. Thales said the origin of things is water, but God is the mind that fashioned everything from water. Here is a reason concerning water and spirit higher and more sublime than any human could have discovered; it was handed down by God. You see the leading philosopher's view in full accord with ours. Anaximenes next, and after him Diogenes of Apollonia, posit air as God, infinite and immense. Their consensus on divinity is likewise similar. Anaxagoras calls the description and motion of the infinite mind God. Pythagoras says God is the soul that pervades the whole nature of things and attends to it, from which the life of all animals is also derived. Xenophanes is known for handing down that all infinite things are God with mind; Antisthenes, that there are many popular gods but one natural and principal God; Zeuxippus [corrected to Speusippus], that the natural, animate power by which all things are governed is known as God. What of Democritus? Although he was the first inventor of atoms, does he not often speak of nature, which crafts images, and intelligence, as God? Strato likewise posits nature; even Epicurus, who either imagines gods as idle or nonexistent, nevertheless sets nature above them. Aristotle varies, yet still assigns a single power: sometimes he calls mind God, sometimes the world, sometimes he places God over the world. Aristotle of Pontus also varies, sometimes attributing the first principle to the world, sometimes to the divine mind. Heraclides of Pontus likewise ascribes the divine mind to God, though in various ways. Theophrastus, Zeno, Chrysippus, and Cleanthes are multiform as well; but they all circle back to the unity of providence. For Cleanthes discusses God as mind, sometimes as soul, sometimes as ether, most often as reason. Zeno, his master, holds that natural and divine law, and sometimes ether, sometimes reason, is the principle of all things. Again, by interpreting Juno as air, Jupiter as heaven, Neptune as sea, fire as Vulcan, and showing the other popular gods to be elements, he seriously indicts and refutes the public error. Chrysippus does much the same: he believes the divine power, rational nature, the world, and fatal necessity are God, and he imitates Zeno's physiological interpretation of the songs of Hesiod, Homer, and Orpheus. The Babylonian Diogenes also teaches the exposition and discussion of Jupiter's birth and Minerva's origin, and that such names are not divine at all. The Socratic Xenophon denies that the form of the true God can be seen, and therefore ought not to be sought. The Stoic Aristo says God cannot be comprehended at all. Both, in their desperation to understand, have sensed the majesty of God. Plato's discourse on God, on things themselves, and on their names is more open; it would be wholly heavenly, were it not sometimes sullied by an admixture of civic persuasion. Accordingly, in the Timaeus, God is the parent of the world, the artificer of the soul, the fabricator of heavenly and earthly things—difficult to find because of his too great and incredible power, and impossible to speak of publicly once found, he says. We have much the same, for we know God and call him the Parent of all, and we never preach publicly unless asked.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the philosophical distinctions and the specific names of the thinkers. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a polished version that correctly incorporates the required scripture/literary citations (Aeneid 6:724–729) which are alluded to in the Latin (Maro). The translation of 'animalem' as 'animate' or 'animal' is consistent with the context of natural power. The handling of the bracketed correction [imp. Spensippum] is correctly addressed in Pass B.
